title: Chetna Organics
subtitle: Building a Farmer-Owned Sustainable Supply Chain — What Mandal Officers Can Learn to Strengthen Their FPOs
audience: Training Session for Mandal Officers • Andhra Pradesh
source_note: Adapted from a Governance Knowledge Centre / OneWorld Foundation India case study

sections.title: Why This Case Study Matters to You
sections.lead: Small and marginal farmers face the same pressures across India — and the same solutions apply to your mandal.

items.title: Poor returns
items.body: Input of Rs. 2000 returned only Rs. 1500 — farming became unviable and farmers quit cotton.

items.title: Exploitation at the mandi
items.body: Middlemen cheated farmers on weight, quality and price; mandi rates often fell below MSP.

items.title: Degraded land
items.body: Heavy chemical use ruined soil health, raising costs season after season.

items.title: No collective strength
items.body: Acting alone, a small farmer had no bargaining power and no access to credit or markets.

sections.title: What Chetna Organics Did
sections.lead: A farmer-owned model combining organic cotton, fair trade and a supply chain fully controlled by farmers.

items.desc: Started as a pilot in Telangana (erstwhile AP) & Maharashtra, facilitated by Solidaridad (a Dutch NGO).
COFA formed by 8 district cooperatives; expanded into Odisha (Kalahandi, Bolangir).
COAPCL — a farmer-owned producer company — set up to market produce directly.

items.label: buyers: Marks & Spencer, H&M, Japan, Denmark

sections.title: The Three-Tier Farmer Structure
sections.lead: Every farmer is simultaneously a member at all levels — ownership and decisions stay with farmers.

tiers.name: Self-Help Group
tiers.desc: 10–20 farmers. Meet monthly on inputs, finance, standards & marketing. Monitor that organic norms are followed.

tiers.name: Cooperative
tiers.desc: 600–700 farmers. A legal entity that can take loans, aggregate produce and hold sub-licence for certification.

tiers.name: Producer Company (COAPCL)
tiers.desc: Farmer-owned trading arm. Sells directly to retailers in India and abroad; holds organic & fair-trade certification.

blocks.closing: Democratic, bottom-up: board members of the producer company are elected from each cooperative.

sections.title: Transforming the Supply Chain
sections.lead: Removing middlemen put control — and margins — back in farmers' hands.

blocks.closing: Farmer loses margin at every hand-off; cheated on weight, quality, price.
blocks.title: BEFORE

blocks.closing: Result: Farmers now earn Rs. 3,950–4,050 per quintal of organic cotton vs Rs. 3,000 market price — and they set the base price.
blocks.title: AFTER (CHETNA MODEL)

sections.title: Four Things That Made It Work
sections.lead: The pillars behind Chetna's success — the elements worth replicating.

items.title: Trust through visible results
items.body: First worked with a few farmers for 2–3 years to prove organic farming lowers input cost and stabilises yield before scaling up.

items.title: A systemised supply chain
items.body: Eliminated middlemen; cooperatives lobbied for their own market place and the producer company linked farmers to buyers.

items.title: A competitive niche
items.body: Organic + fair trade created exclusivity. Organic farming saved ~Rs. 4,000 per acre by cutting chemical inputs.

items.title: Long-term buyer relationships
items.body: Direct ties with retailers, quality assurance, sample sharing, and barcode traceability of every batch.

sections.title: Lessons for Strengthening Your FPO
sections.lead: What a mandal officer can act on

items.title: Start small, build genuine ownership
items.body: Form tight SHGs of 10–20 farmers that meet monthly. Federate them upward. Let farmers make the decisions, so the FPO truly belongs to them.

items.title: Demonstrate before you scale
items.body: Run a small demo plot for 2–3 seasons. Visible results convert sceptical farmers far better than a meeting ever will.

items.title: Aggregate to gain bargaining power
items.body: Pool produce through the FPO so members negotiate as one. Use the APMC reforms to create your own collection point and skip exploitative middlemen.

items.title: Build a niche & certification
items.body: Help the FPO move into organic, GI or fair-trade lines where margins are higher. Certification and traceability (e.g. barcoding) command premium prices.

items.title: Forge direct, lasting buyer links
items.body: Connect the FPO to institutional and export buyers. Direct relationships and assured quality replace one-off, low-price mandi sales.

items.title: Make it self-sustaining & transparent
items.body: Use trade profits to fund certification and operations. Build internal control systems and bottom-up monitoring so the FPO outlives any subsidy or officer.

sections.title: Your Role as a Mandal Officer
sections.lead: A practical checklist to take back to the field.

items.title: Identify & mobilise
items.body: Map willing small/marginal farmers; help them form and register SHGs and cooperatives.

items.title: Enable, don't control
items.body: Facilitate meetings and capacity-building; keep ownership and voting with farmers.

items.title: Link to schemes & credit
items.body: Connect the FPO to institutional credit, insurance, NREGS works and govt. schemes.

items.title: Open markets
items.body: Use APMC reforms; help set up collection centres and connect to bulk/export buyers.

items.title: Add value
items.body: Push for organic / certified / processed lines that earn a premium over raw produce.

items.title: Ensure transparency
items.body: Set up simple internal monitoring so members trust the system and it stays sustainable.

sections.title: When farmers own the supply chain, they capture the value.
sections.source: Adapted from Governance Knowledge Centre / OneWorld Foundation India — Chetna Organics Case Study (Feb 2011)

blocks.text: A strong FPO is not built by an officer issuing orders — it is built by helping farmers organise, prove the model on the ground, and connect directly to markets. That is how Chetna turned abandoned cotton fields into a premium, farmer-owned business.
